title: ‘South Park’ Takes Aim at Jensen Huang, Nvidia Spy Scandal in Next Episode
full_text: Skip to main content By James Hibberd Plus Icon James Hibberd Writer-at-Large JamesHibberd Follow Sign Up View All November 24, 2026 12:00pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'South Park' Logo text The espionage allegations surrounding Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and America’s recent series of software outages and cyberattacks appear to be the next cultural targets to be mocked on South Park (rebranded South America for the current season). Wednesday’s episode is titled “City Endings.” The official description reads: “When mysterious power outages strike South America, the townspeople fear Chinese cyberattacks. It’s up to the boys to discover what’s really going on.” In a brief promo for the episode (watch it below), a local declares, “Someone in this town is a Chinese spy.” In another scene, Tuong Lu Kim, also known as the City Wok Guy, is announcing the grand opening of his new massage parlor called City Massage (a name which takes on a different meaning when you hear how co-creator Trey Parker voices it). Related Stories Business The Center of the News Universe Has Shifted to CNBC Business Nvidia Board Reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO The new episode will have its debut on Comedy Central at 10 p.m. ET and will stream on Thursday on Paramount+. South Park is coming off last year’s Emmy-winning season, which also set some modern-day ratings records for the show. The show has made appearances in the Nielsen streaming Top 10 this season but has come down a bit from last year’s highs, when the show pivoted into a series of topical attacks on the Trump administration. The series rebranded as South America to mock President Trump’s penchant for trying to rename geographic features. Check out the promo below for Wednesday’s episode below. THR

title: Kevin Kline Boards ‘The Corrections’ at Netflix
full_text: Skip to main content By Rick Porter Plus Icon Rick Porter Television Business Editor rickporter Follow Sign Up View All November 24, 2026 12:00pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Kevin Kline Dia Dipasupil/Getty Images Logo text Netflix is adding a second Oscar winner to the cast of The Corrections . Kevin Kline will star opposite Meryl Streep in the limited series adaptation of Jonathan Franzen’s novel. The series will be an on-screen reunion for Kline and Streep, who have appeared together in the feature films Sophie’s Choice (Kline’s film debut), A Prairie Home Companion and Ricki and the Flash . In The Corrections , Kline will play Alfred Lambert, the patriarch of the family at the center of the story. The character is “a man of strict principles and old-fashioned decorum” who is “battling the afflictions of aging,” Netflix’s description reads. “Alfred must come to terms with his three very modern children — a daughter whose secrets he can no longer protect, an older son who has displaced him as the authority in the family, and a wayward son whose forgiveness he yearns for.” Related Stories Business Bela Bajaria Calls Time at Netflix a "Fun Chapter" as She Teases Rest and "Conversations" in First Remarks on Exit Movies Sadie Sandler to Star in Netflix Horror Movie 'Malibu' From Vertigo, Happy Madison (Exclusive) Streep, who has been attached to the project since it went into development in 2024, is playing Enid Lambert, the family matriarch and Alfred’s wife. The series will follow the three adult siblings who “desperately resist their mother’s wish for one last Christmas together — each undone by the delusional ambitions that were supposed to save them from becoming their parents.” Paramount TV Studios is producing The Corrections . Franzen is adapting his best-selling and National Book Award-winning 2001 novel. Cord Jefferson ( American Fiction, Watchmen ) will direct every episode. They executive produce with Mark Roybal and Paul Lee of Wiip, Nicole Clemens, Amy Sayres and Streep. Kline won the best supporting actor Oscar in 1989 for his role in A Fish Called Wanda . He’s coming off the MGM+ series American Classic and has a recurring voice role on Bob’s Burgers (for which he earned an Emmy nomination in 2017). His credits also include Apple TV’s Disclaimer and feature films Dave, In & Out and The Big Chill . Kline is repped by UTA and Berwick & Kovacik. THR

title: ‘The Spiral’ Director Paolo Strippoli Talks Oscar-Buzzed Horror Pic: “I Try to Lower Expectations”
full_text: × Skip to main content By Etan Vlessing Plus Icon Etan Vlessing Canada Bureau Chief View All November 24, 2026 11:58am Add us as a Google Preferred Source L-R) Jasmine Trinca, Romana Maggiora Vergano, Valeria Bruni Tedeschi, Adriano Giannini and Paolo Strippoli attend the 'Spiral' screening during the 83rd Venice International Film Festival. Aurore Marechal Paolo Strippoli has been making waves on the festival circuit, starting with Venice , where his psychological horror thriller The Spiral ( L’Estranea ) debuted. Now, he is leading an awards season campaign for Italy’s official Oscar entry for Best International Film. But after Fellini, a Hollywood darling, Giuseppe Tornatore, Roberto Benigni, Paola Sorentino earlier won Oscar trophies with their movies, the Italian genre specialist is paving a new road to possible gold statues for his country with early buzz and prestigious awards. Ahead of an awards season screening of The Spiral for Academy voters in Toronto on Tuesday night, Strippoli talked to The Hollywood Reporter about what he wants to avoid and get right as he shows off his critically and commercially successful thriller. Related Stories Business "Alarming" Diversity Backtrack Happening In Film and TV Industry In Canada, Report Finds TV Why Mike Flanagan Just Couldn't Kill Carrie White And that includes curbing aspirations. “We know we have strong contenders. So as we go on, and the competition grows, it’s risky for your well-being. So I try to lower expectations. I try to enjoy this time meeting people, showing the film in different countries,” Strippoli explained. His low expectations could, however, be a tactical advantage as the Oscar campaign for The Spiral, backed by the Italian government and industry, looks to advance by exceeding predictions for the best international film competition. In many ways, The Spiral has come out of nowhere to earn Oscar contention. After his third feature, Holy Boy, premiered out of competition in Venice, festival artistic director Alberto Barbera blessed with a competition berth Strippoli’s fourth feature and escalating horror pic about a wife and mother taking her family to ever-darker places over a fear of an imperfect family. In Venice, the hometown audience gave Strippoli and his cast – including Jasmine Trinca, Valeria Bruni Tedeschi, Romana Maggiora Vergano, Adriano Giannini and Andrea Genovese – a nine-minute standing ovation and strong reviews, and that was followed by the horror thriller voted the first runner-up for the People’s Choice Midnight Madness Award at the Toronto Film Festival. It didn’t take long after that for The Spiral starring Trinca as a mother drawn into a Faustian pact with a mysterious stranger played by Bruni Tedeschi to be tapped as Italy’s submission for the best international feature Oscar, and the first for a homegrown genre film. “I’m very proud because it’s my movie, but I also interpret this as a great signal for genre cinema in Italy, and we’re fighting to go further as possible to hopefully make it to the short list,” Strippoli said. The director, who co-wrote the film’s screenplay with Salvatore De Chirico, kicks off his horror movie with a generational fight between Trinca as Anna, a frantic mother confessing a lie to Alice, her estranged daughter played by Maggiora Vergano, that she insists destroyed her family — and while all dark rainstorm rages out the apartment window. “I care about the intimate story of the characters, but what really fascinates me is how I can talk about the outside world, the whole society around these characters,” Strippoli explained of the raw emotions of the mother and daughter in the apartment corresponding to an intensifying Biblical flood outside. Their family’s downfall over 25 years unfolds in The Spiral across four chapters, centered on a Faustian bargain between Anna and The Stranger (Bruni Tedeschi). Strippoli and co-writer De Chirico deliberately crafted The Stranger not as a dark, Satanic figure, but as a mischievous entity who gracefully exploits the greed and cunning of the affluent Anna. “It was beautiful to work with them,” Strippoli said in praise of Trinca and Bruni Tedschi. “I wanted their relationship to be carnal, sapphic. Because Anna is so stiff in everyday life, and when she is with The Stranger, for her it’s a liberating experience,” the director explained. Theatrical audiences have responded to this tale of a desperate housewife and her graceful messenger of evil. The Venice competition launch and buzz also helped lift The Spiral to surpassing $4 million at the Italian box office since bowing on Oct. 8. Strippoli’s film also had a Nov. 17 screening in Los Angeles for Oscar voters just as the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences after the Thanksgiving break gets set to draw up an Oscar shortlist for best international feature. Spain’s La Bola Negra is the heavy favorite, but Strippoli’s Italian backers are betting The Spiral can move up behind leaders like Romania’s Palme d’Or winner Fjord , France’s Minotaur and South Korea’s Possible Love to make the shortlist of 15 films to be announced on Dec. 15. In the meantime, New Line Cinema has won a competitive bid for the English language remake rights to The Spiral, a deal that includes the Paramount label also getting distribution rights to the Italian film in North America and a host of international territories. New Line also plans a limited theatrical release for the Italian-language film before the end of 2026 to ensure Oscar season contention. The Spiral filmmakers have inevitably received Hollywood horror scripts from major studios and streamers looking for the next Backrooms and Obsession after the summer breakout box office success of those thriller chillers. But as he looks to drive award season attention for his film, Strippoli said he needs balance commercial expectations with creative ambitions. “Every time I work on something, I don’t do so with expectations. Of course I deal with expectations. But in my job, in my work, expectations can change the nature of a project for the worse,” he warns. Strippoli said trying to match creative expectations with a producer’s commercial assumptions risks ending in failure. “I won’t succeed, and my movie will worse than it should be and could be,” he argued. For that reason, Strippoli insists on an authenticity and honesty in his work to better his chances of connecting with and speaking to audiences. “I think people value honesty and people need be contradicted at times. They want to be surprised. They don’t want to be treated like children. They are paying for a vision and you have to give a vision, so expectations are never good,” he adds. So while Strippoli hinted at one his next movies possibly being another genre pic, and even an English language film for a more diverse cast, he’s also looking beyond an Oscar race for The Spiral for his next finished script and adventure on a film set. “I really miss the set. I really love the family you build on set. And finally seeing what you imagined coming to life and it’s beautiful,” he said. THR

title: Andrew Scott on Starring in ‘Elsinore’ and Feeling ‘Very Grateful’ to Be an Out Gay Actor
full_text: × Continue to Variety SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Nov 24, 2026 11:36am PT Andrew Scott on Starring in ‘Elsinore’ and Feeling ‘Very Grateful’ to Be an Out Gay Actor By Marc Malkin Plus Icon Marc Malkin Senior Editor, Culture and Events marcmalkin Latest Andrew Scott on Starring in ‘Elsinore’ and Feeling ‘Very Grateful’ to Be an Out Gay Actor 10 minutes ago ‘Artificial’ Writer Simon Rich Boards Oscar-Qualified Sci-Fi Short ‘Houston, We Have a Crush’ as Executive Producer (EXCLUSIVE) 4 days ago Jennifer Lopez Wears 186-Carat Diamond Necklace to ‘JLo Show’ Premiere: ‘There’s Security All Around’ 4 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source ©Focus Features/Courtesy Everett Collection Andrew Scott remembers first learning about HIV and AIDS when he was growing up in Dublin, Ireland. “I would have been incredibly young, but I remember Oprah Winfrey talking about it,” he tells me. “She did quite a lot. She had Magic Johnson. That was a little bit later, but I remember she had Magic Johnson on her show and she spoke about the crisis. She had people who were living with HIV. It seemed kind of far away at the time.” Related Stories ‘PAW Patrol’ Spinoff Series ‘Skye’s Pup Squad’ Set for 2027 Release Scott is now at the center of the conversation because of his starring role in “ Elsinore .” He plays Ian Charleson , a star of the 1981 Oscar-winning “Chariots of Fire,” who starred in a 1989 production of “Hamlet” at the National Theatre in London as he was dying of AIDS. Charleson never publicly revealed his sexuality or his illness before passing away just weeks after completing his run in “Hamlet.” Scott came out in 2013 in an interview with “The Independent.” “I relate to it deeply, and I relate to it as a professional who wants to just do my job and as somebody who feels very grateful to get those opportunities that Ian and his counterparts didn’t,” says Scott, who is considered a front-runner in the Oscar race for best actor. “I feel celebratory that I can look around and that there are out gay actors who are growing in number and not placing us in this insidious heaviness burden about separating actors in that way. It feels really wonderful that we have a lot of out gay actors in the movie in a movie about there not being a lot of out gay actors.” Director Simon Stone says casting an openly gay actor as Charleson was “hugely important.” “I think what message that sends to the world is that times have changed, and that we’re not going to apologize for the story that we’re telling here,” he says. “Andrew has had the huge benefit of the pioneering work of so many actors before him, that his career was not disadvantaged at all by being openly gay. He’s probably the first generation of actors who can say that.” Ian Charleson in “Chariots of Fire.” 20th Century Fox Licensing/Merchandising / Everett Collection “Elsinore” also stars Billie Piper as Patsy, Charleson’s best friend who took care of him through his illness. Piper remembers Stone being mindful of how heavy that subject matter was. “It was a very sensitive set. Simon was very good at setting a very peaceful environment,” Piper says. “People were in their socks, sort of padding around. It felt like a womb. It felt like a nest. People could be extremely emotional. I think a lot of the crew were very upset watching takes. I think for the actors sometimes you’re so adrenalized that you’re sort of just in it. Reflection is something that sometimes comes later.” The “Elsinore” cast also includes Olivia Colman as Charleson’s physician, Dr. Margaret Johnson, David Dawson as filmmaker Derek Jarman and Joe Locke as a fellow AIDS patient. Screenwriter Stephen Beresford’s research included talking to the real “fantastically generous” Patsy as well as many other people who knew Charleson. “Some of the people I spoke to are not in great health now, who are older,” Beresford says. “But they made the effort to come and talk to me because they wanted to honor Ian, and that’s very special.” As Charleson’s health deteriorates in the film, he develops Kaposi sarcoma lesions on his skin. Scott says he tried not to pay attention to the transfer tattoos that makeup department head Nadia Stacey applied to his skin to duplicate the dark cancerous growths. “In some ways, a little bit like Ian, I had to try and think, ‘Well, they aren’t there.’ He did what he had to do, but he was determined with getting on with the business of living,” Scott says. “He threw himself into ‘Hamlet,’ and I threw myself into ‘Elsinore.’ It was very important to me to not fetishize Ian’s death, but to really think about his living. If everybody else was playing the tragedy around him, he was certainly looking toward the light and in some ways I tried to mirror that.” Meanwhile, you can also watch Scott talking about Charleson and the making of “Elsinore” with Oprah Winfrey on the latest episode of “The Oprah Podcast.” ‘Friends’ Cast Entered Matthew Perry’s Funeral Holding Hands and Cried Around the Casket, Netflix Documentary Reveals David Schwimmer Reunites With His Famous Red Sweater From ‘Friends’ in Nostalgic Quince Campaign Loading comments...

title: ‘Hexed’ Creatives on Telling a Modern-Day Witchcraft Story, Casting Hailee Steinfeld, and Their Favorite Easter Eggs
full_text: Continue to Variety SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Nov 24, 2026 11:32am PT ‘Hexed’ Creatives on Telling a Modern-Day Witchcraft Story, Casting Hailee Steinfeld, and Their Favorite Easter Eggs By Jazz Tangcay Plus Icon Jazz Tangcay Artisans Editor @jazzt Latest Inside the Macy’s Thanksgiving Parade at 100: Massive Minions, K-Pop Stars and ‘Sorcerer’s Apprentice’ Mickey Mouse 20 hours ago How the ‘Elsinore’ Makeup Team Transformed Stars Andrew Scott and Olivia Colman to Bring the Story of Ian Charleson to Life 3 days ago ‘Being Heumann’ Producers Team With Marc Furmie, Rezistor Films on Cult Comic ‘Deadworld’ Film — Film News in Brief 4 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Disney SPOILER ALERT: This story discusses mild plot points for “ Hexed ,” opening in theaters on Wednesday. Walt Disney Animation Studios’ 65th film “Hexed” tells the story of the hidden world of witches and how, throughout history, they have been misunderstood. At its heart, however, is a story of motherhood and the powerful bond between a mother and daughter. Disney animated films often kill off a parent to propel a story forward. But the creatives behind “Hexed” embraced that important relationship. Related Stories ‘PAW Patrol’ Spinoff Series ‘Skye’s Pup Squad’ Set for 2027 Release Directed by Fawn Veerasunthorn and Jason Hand, and co-directed by Josie Trinidad, the film follows Billie ( Hailee Steinfeld ), a rebellious teen who escapes into the secret world of Hexe, a realm of witches and wizards who live in harmony with nature. Veerasunthorn explained that the story idea was originally pitched by Trinidad. “She wanted to tell a story about the hidden world of witches. What if there’s a place where they can thrive on their own? The place built by witches for witches.” More importantly, Veerasunthorn notes, Trinidad wanted to tell a story of motherhood and the true heart of the story lies in the complicated, relatable relationship between Billie and her mother, Alice (Rashida Jones). In developing Billie, she was portrayed as a modern teenager who wears combat boots and has an edgy style. Producer Yvett Merino explains that Billie oozes confidence: “She doesn’t quite fit in. There’s something that feels different about her.” The key was making the film’s main protagonist relatable. “We all go through that at some point in our lives, especially in those teenage years where you’re just trying to figure out who you are,” Merino says. “She takes her mom’s car. She borrows her mom’s car to go and free the school mascot. She’s imperfect, impulsive and maybe doesn’t always make the best decisions.” Merino goes on to say, “When I was a teenager, I didn’t always make the best decisions. But you know what? I got away with it. We’ll just learn from that lesson.” Imperfect relationships were key when it came to Alice as well. Alice is protective of Billie and wants to keep her daughter safe. Hand points out, “We’re all imperfect. We’re all trying our hardest, but we’re still figuring it out and that was really important to us.” Baby Billie Doe and Alice Disney Visually, the world of “Hexed” is vibrant and it took over 700 artists to bring it to life, sometimes with up to 40 people working on a sequence. “The animation style pushed boundaries as far as they could by creating a world audiences had not seen before, filled with characters they’d never seen,” Veerasunthorn says. The idea was that it would feel like a crisp autumn day after it had just rained and the air felt a bit chilly. “It’s a perfect place where magic can thrive,” she adds. Producer Roy Conli credits the film’s production designer, Lorelay Bové, for her creativity. “When people see this film, they will see a world they’ve never seen; they’ll see characters they’ve never seen before in a Disney film.” If the textures of Hexe look heightened, that was a deliberate choice. “We turn the dial up so it feels more like a caricature drawing could feel,” Hand explains. “We wanted this world to be so enticing to Billie. All of our decisions within the world of Hexe go back to Billie. When she goes out into that city for the first time, what’s she going to want to see? Why is this world built for her? What is it speaking to her inside?” Hand says. All those factors were important from both a production design standpoint, but also from a character standpoint. “And then for that journey to bring her mom back into it, throws her for a loop. That’s where the story starts to get its juice and interesting.” Voice casting was important too. Hand recalls seeing Steinfeld in “True Grit” and later in “The Edge of Seventeen.” In that film, Steinfeld plays a troubled teen who had a contentious relationship with their mom. He says, “I always loved her in that role. I still loved her, even though she was doing the worst things and saying terrible stuff and that’s a really great quality.” But it was her voice quality that made her perfect to lead “Hexed.” “Our animators even picked up on particular mannerisms of the way she holds her mouth, little micro expressions that she does.” Jones was perfect for Alice. Verasunthorn says, “Rashida brings this sense of comedy in a very uptight mom. Those two words don’t go well together, but somehow she makes it work. The depth of vulnerability that we get to see in Alice is quite beautiful.” “Hexed” wouldn’t be a Disney movie without a villain to stir up a little trouble. Enter Jodie Foster, who voices Queen Celeste, a sinister ruler who stops at nothing to maintain her power. Was it easy to get her to say yes? Conli says, “We asked her and she did it. She’d never played a villain before. She’s done a phenomenal job at this incredible narcissistic witch that is a little over the top.” Queen Celeste is voiced by Jodie Foster. Disney Joining Steinfeld, Jones and Foster are Walton Goggins as Beef Roger Krumchuk, a three-eyed cat. “He brought so much comedy and so much personality, way beyond what we ever imagined,” Merino says. Billie Doe and Beef Roger Crummchuk Disney As for the film’s Easter eggs, there are plenty to look out for. Among them are Aladdin’s magic carpet in Billie’s bedroom, a floating head fortuneteller that nods to “The Haunted Mansion.” Mother Gothel from “Tangled” appears in a blink-and-you’ll-miss-it moment. Hand’s favorite one is Cursula, a nod to “The Little Mermaid’s” Ursula. “It’s voiced by Jodi Benson — who provided the voice of Ariel in the original animated film. I love ‘The Little Mermaid’ so much, and so to have Jodi Benson come in and do a complete twist on it and have her play Cursula, she was so amazing. She gave us such energy.” Merino and Conli concur that the scene with dancing brooms is one that is special for both of them. “It reaches back to our history and goes back to Walt Disney’s “Fantasia,” and the Sorcerer’s Apprentice scene,” Merino says. “The brooms, that’s 80 years in the past. That’s ‘Fantasia’; it touches on this amazing legacy that we all live with, and we all celebrate.” David Schwimmer Reunites With His Famous Red Sweater From ‘Friends’ in Nostalgic Quince Campaign ‘Friends’ Cast Entered Matthew Perry’s Funeral Holding Hands and Cried Around the Casket, Netflix Documentary Reveals Loading comments...

title: ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’ Album’s Secret Weapon? The ‘Barbie’ Soundtrack Creator
full_text: × Skip to main content By Ethan Millman Plus Icon Ethan Millman Music Editor View All November 24, 2026 11:28am Add us as a Google Preferred Source The Jason and Lucia characters in 'Grand Theft Auto VI.' Rockstar Games For the biggest game the studio has ever released, Grand Theft Auto VI developer Rockstar Games wanted an equally ambitious soundtrack. Like much of the entertainment business these days, they turned to Atlantic Records to help make that happen. Over the past decade, the record label’s soundtrack efforts, spearheaded by Atlantic Music Group President Kevin Weaver, have established Atlantic as the de-facto landing spot for media companies looking to build a star-studded accompanying album for their work. Since 2015, Atlantic has handled the soundtracks for movies including Furious 7, Suicide Squad, Greatest Showman, F1, Twisters and most-famously Barbie, the latter of which became a cultural phenomenon alongside the film itself. But the biggest opportunity Atlantic has seen to this point wasn’t a movie, but rather a video game. “I went to Rockstar and said that they control the most culturally relevant IP on the planet, and that what they do with music is incredible,” Weaver told The Hollywood Reporter over the phone from Miami — where he’d spent much of last week attending launch events for the game — as he recalled the initial pitch to the company. “Music is such an endemic part of the game and what GTA is. Why don’t we endeavor to do something similar to what I’d done on Barbie and these other soundtracks and A&R a whole lot of new records? ” Weaver produced the soundtrack along with fellow Atlantic execs Joseph Khoury, Cody Verdecias, and Brandon Davis. GTA marked new territory for Weaver, the first time he’d taken on a video game soundtrack, which as he acknowledges, wasn’t on his purview before the game came into the fold. “I’d never been interested in doing a video game soundtrack, to be honest with you,” Weaver says. “We license a lot of music to games, and I’ve had plenty of game companies come to me over the years, but if I’m not moving the needle and elevating the next thing I do, I’m not doing it. This was a natural choice, this was the one.” Similar to the process with film soundtracks, early on, Rockstar showed Atlantic some key scenes from the game they wanted music for that were mostly set to temp tracks to help show the overall tone and feel they were looking for. Among the first artists they reached out to, Weaver says, was Travis Scott, with some of the other earlier asks including Morgan Wallen and Dua Lipa. Scott, Weaver says, turned in the first song, with “Rhyno,” one of the soundtrack’s initial singles. Another Scott track, “Burn This Shit Down,” plays prominently during a key mission in chapter one. The official soundtrack itself is just one aspect in the wider, rich musical world Rockstar has created for GTA VI. French electronic duo Justice, for example, provided the game’s score. GTA’s musical lifeblood, though, is the game’s radio stations, which feature hundreds of songs across two dozen channels, hosted by real-life celebrities like Robyn, Wallen, Bad Bunny, Keith Richards and Lana Del Rey among many more. Atlantic didn’t handle the radio stations, but Weaver says the company and Rockstar were “attached at the hip,” and some of those soundtrack offers came simultaneously with asks for the stars to host the radio shows. Rockstar’s vision wasn’t set on any one genre, with the soundtrack spanning country, rock, hip-hop, blues, pop, electronic and latin among other genres. Just days into release, two of the game’s needle drops have gone viral, with the game breathing new life into Carly Rae Jepsen’s cult classic “When the Lights Go Out” and Dire Straits’ “Money For Nothing.” (Neither of those songs is on the official soundtrack, but they play in key missions in the game’s first two chapters.) Jepsen has already re-released her song, hoping to build off the momentum and finally land it on the Hot 100. “Something Rockstar identified to us right away — this isn’t a rap game,” Weaver says. “It’s not a country game or dance music game. All of this music lives within the game in so many different facets, and that gives us a great opportunity to go out and create records across pretty much every genre we want. It’s GTA’s taste and tone that makes this work.” The only real through-line, Weaver says, was capturing what he refers to as “the glitz and grime” of Vice City and Leonida, the game’s stand-ins for Miami and the broader Florida area. While Atlantic’s more than used to handling a rollout for a film soundtrack, the strategy for video games is significantly different. While a movie’s lifespan in the immediate zeitgeist is typically a few weeks — pre-release marketing, the main theatrical window and post-theater streaming — a video game like GTA will hold a captive audience for years. GTA V had a dedicated audience for 13 years before the latest game finally came out last week. “The tail on this never ends,” Weaver says. “Records are being discovered in the game in real time right now as the game is coming to market as it’s come to market in the last 24 hours, so we kind of have an opportunity to see which records really start to raise their hand as well.” In the days since the game came out, Rockstar and Atlantic already surprise released a deluxe version of the soundtrack with 23 more songs atop the original 34, and today, they dropped four more songs from 100 gecs, Favored Nations, Joe Armon-Jones and Alex Frankel as iTunes exclusives. As for any more musical plans going forward, Weaver says “the world’s just gonna have to wait and see.” THR

title: ‘Naughty’ vs ‘Nasty’: Universal and Warner Bros. Battle Over Titles for New Jennifer Aniston, Jenna Ortega Movies (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: × Continue to Variety SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Nov 24, 2026 11:24am PT ‘Naughty’ vs ‘Nasty’: Universal and Warner Bros. Battle Over Titles for New Jennifer Aniston, Jenna Ortega Movies (EXCLUSIVE) By Matt Donnelly , Rebecca Rubin Add us as a Google Preferred Source Michael Buckner / NOAM GALAI 6469571282 Two similarly titled movies are causing a war of words between Universal and Warner Bros . Pictures. The legacy studios are locked in a stalemate over dueling projects that sound alike and are set to hit theaters around the same time, five sources tell Variety . The first is “ Naughty ,” Olivia Wilde’s raucous Christmas comedy starring Jennifer Aniston. The other is “ Nasty ,” Mary Bronstein’s psychological drama led by Jenna Ortega, which will roll out under Warner’s new indie label Clockwork. Universal slated “Naughty” for Nov. 5, 2027, after registering the name with the Motion Picture Association in 2023, according to two sources. Clockwork, the nascent shingle run by Neon veteran Christian Parkes, has not officially set a date for “Nasty,” though four sources say the film is also eyeing a November 2027 release. Related Stories ‘PAW Patrol’ Spinoff Series ‘Skye’s Pup Squad’ Set for 2027 Release Generally, studios go to great lengths to avoid delivering movies with similar-sounding names — much less launching them in the same corridor. “Naughty” and “Nasty” aren’t alike in genre or subject matter. “Naughty,” featuring Aniston and Peter Dinklage, follows a single mom who has to convince Santa Claus to testify at her divorce hearing. “Nasty,” Bronstein’s follow-up to “If I Had Legs I’d Kick You,” revolves around an elite gymnast competing for a spot on the Olympic team while dealing with her manipulative coach. Yet insiders at Universal and Warner Bros. feel the fact that the titles are basically synonyms could confuse moviegoers. Further complicating the matter is that LuckyChap, Margot Robbie’s prolific film and TV production shop, is backing both projects. Universal and Clockwork declined to comment. The spat is headed toward a formal review by the MPA, which has a 101-year-old department called the Title Registration Bureau to manage such conflicts. Arbitration involves a panel of studio intellectual property lawyers at the ready to hash it out. Although titles are not copyrightable, the TRB is armed with a 50-page document outlining rules of play and precedent, per one source, and its rulings are legally binding. The MPA declined to comment on the matter. “Movies want to distinguish themselves, and the first way they do that is the title,” says Jeff Bock, an analyst with Exhibitor Relations. “If they sound similar, there could be confusion.” Universal believes it should have dibs since it was first to file with “Naughty.” That would mean “Nasty” either changes its name or shifts its release date. Insiders note Clockwork filed two alternative titles for “Nasty” with its MPA documentation, but the filmmakers are against using the backups. Meanwhile, sources close to “Nasty” feel that Universal is “punching down” at Clockwork because the indie drama doesn’t have the same broad commercial appeal as the Aniston-led holiday comedy. (Though Clockwork is a specialty label, it is owned and operated by the vast Skydance Motion Picture Group). Wilde is content to let “Nasty” proceed as titled, according to a person familiar with her thinking. LuckyChap is working toward a solution that sets up both projects for success without entering MPA arbitration, two sources add. Disputes like these rarely become public knowledge, insiders say. And most often, studios work it out without involving the Title Registration Bureau. The group’s last two arbitrations were in 2018. That’s when Disney and Lucasfilm settled on “Solo: A Star Wars Story” rather than “Solo” to distinguish the Han Solo origin story from the 2018 climbing documentary “Free Solo.” And Universal agreed to change its raunchy comedy to “Blockers” from “The Pact,” a name that was already used by a 2012 horror film. Renaming movies can benefit both parties. Ask Paramount and Sony, which released “No Strings Attached” and “Friends With Benefits” a few months apart in 2011. Both romantic comedies — one starring Natalie Portman and Ashton Kutcher and the other with Mila Kunis and Justin Timberlake — had an identical premise involving two friends who agree to casual sex without dating. “No Strings Attached” was originally called “Friends With Benefits,” but the studio acquiesced to the title change. Any plot similarities didn’t dilute the films’ respective box office, with each one grossing $149 million globally. To that end, movies with similar themes or ideas are less of a problem for studios. Bock points to 1998’s “Armageddon” and “Deep Impact,” two disaster films about comets on a collision course with Earth. Both were theatrical winners, with “Armageddon” earning $553 million globally and “Deep Impact” generating $350 million globally. “Consumers might be fooled by something like that, but it didn’t affect the box office,” he says. “They turned out to be different, even though the synopsis was the same.” David Schwimmer Reunites With His Famous Red Sweater From ‘Friends’ in Nostalgic Quince Campaign ‘Friends’ Cast Entered Matthew Perry’s Funeral Holding Hands and Cried Around the Casket, Netflix Documentary Reveals Loading comments...

title: Montel Williams Gets Candid About the State of Daytime TV: “The Talk Shows of My Era Became the Reality Shows of Today”
full_text: × Skip to main content By Kimberly Nordyke Plus Icon Kimberly Nordyke Managing Editor, Digital View All November 24, 2026 11:22am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Montel Williams JC Olivera/Variety/Getty Images Montel Williams is getting candid about the state of daytime talk show, saying viewers’ attention spans have changed a lot since he ended his own talker in 2008. “It’s a sad commentary that we lost our attention span in the last 15 years,” he said in a conversation with We’re Out of Time podcast host Richard Taite, debuting Tuesday. “The talk shows that I did and the talk shows of that era were hourlong talk discussions. We don’t have the patience anymore to listen to a topic for an hour. I say the majority of people don’t.” Related Stories TV 'Property Brother' Jonathan Scott Is Getting a Daytime Talk Show TV Montel Williams Hospitalized After Workout, Spokesman Says He said the format has morphed quite a bit since his show ended. ( The Montel Williams Show ran from July 1991 to May 2008, spanning 17 seasons.) “So the talk shows of my era became the reality shows of today,” he opined. “I’ll say that again, the talk shows of my era became the reality shows of today. We took the dysfunction that we put on display and turned those into individual shows of their own, to the point now that the talk that’s out there right now, what do they really even talk? Other than selling products and hawking a new movie or hawking a new record, what do they do? Is there any discussion that makes man better?” Williams was quick to say he’s not criticizing anyone in particular, just nothing how times have changed. “I’m not casting aspersion on my peers of the day,” he said. “But I am saying that at least back when we talked about issues, we talked about issues that changed the world, that I believe changed America. We were talking about AIDS before any news stations were going full reports on it. We were talking about civil unrest, we were talking about racism, we were talking about hate, we were talking about all those things that we didn’t even talk about it around the dinner table. We talked about it. Some of us did it in the salacious way. But at least they had a discussion.” Williams added that the goal with his show was to educate people and put a spotlight on a topic that viewers perhaps hadn’t been introduced to or thought that much about. In other words, something that would “make you stop and think,” he said. Does he think that kind of talk show would work today? “It could, if it was formatted differently,” he says. “I think we can go an entire hour, but we have to go in that hour introducing every single piece of that topic, not just one piece, but we have to introduce it all and add to it information that people can take away.” Taite likened that to scrolling on your phone, where you’re staying engaged by absorbing different information — and a lot of it — in a short time span. “That’s right, and [keeping] you stimulated on the same topic instead of scrolling, or swiping up and down, instead of doing that and getting a different topic every single second, and that’s what they’re trying to do,” Williams replied. “They’re trying to give you something different every five or six minutes where they never really even solved the first five minutes. I say that every single topic out there can be broken into 20 different topics. Somebody needs to just program it that way.” He added, “I think we may gravitate back to that as soon as we realize that we pushed attention span to a point where it’s no longer attention span.” Watch the clip below. The full episode of We’re Out of Time with Montel Williams and host Richard Taite premieres at noon PT on Tuesday on YouTube, Spotify and Apple Podcasts. THR

title: ‘Clashing Through The Snow’ Director Carlson Young Breaks Down Buc-ee’s Knockoff, Ryan’s Counsel From Chat GPT & Her Way Into The “Holiday Hijinks” Rom-Com
full_text: Skip to main content By Dessi Gomez Dessi Gomez SEO Staff Writer @GomezDessi More Stories By Dessi ‘Clashing Through The Snow’ Stars Christopher Briney & Michelle Randolph Talk Comedy’s “Important” Presence In Script And How They Built Their Characters All The Songs In ‘Clashing Through The Snow’ From Sabrina Carpenter To Olivia Rodrigo Everything We Know About Amazon MGM & Sony Pictures TV’s ‘God Of War’ Adaptation So Far View All November 24, 2026 11:18am Add us as a Google Preferred Source L-R: Chris Briney and Michelle Randolph in 'Clashing Through the Snow' and director Carlson Young Prime Video/Nick Rasmussen Clashing Through the Snow director Carlson Young found it easy to relate to the film’s two main characters, Ryan Mitchell ( Christopher Briney ) and Hannah Hendricks ( Michelle Randolph ). The story centers the pair, two senior editors competing to oust the other from a condensed role due to impending layoffs, chasing big book deals for the publishing company where they work. Ryan operates off of commercial motivation and tapping into what is popular to sell books while Hannah identifies as more of a literary purist who takes big swings with the depth of books she takes on. Related Stories News All The Songs In ‘Clashing Through The Snow’ From Sabrina Carpenter To Olivia Rodrigo News ‘Clashing Through The Snow’ Stars Christopher Briney & Michelle Randolph Talk Comedy’s “Important” Presence In Script And How They Built Their Characters “[The script] really spoke to me. I felt so connected to Hannah and Ryan’s literary perspectives, and it felt like a existential conversation that I have with myself, moment to moment, constantly,” Young told Deadline. “It was easy for me to access their personalities and their inner worlds. And then I just loved the classic, holiday hijinks that ensue from there, and I was up for the challenge of trying to make a great holiday rom-com.” Watch on Deadline The director connected the differing stances on what sells to challenges she navigates in her own job “balancing art and commerce, and what is and isn’t viable in storytelling and in the marketplace.”

title: Bill Maher and Byron Allen to Be Honored at Los Angeles City College Foundation Gala
full_text: × Skip to main content By Chris Gardner Plus Icon Chris Gardner chrissgardner Follow Sign Up View All November 24, 2026 11:10am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Byron Allen and Bill Maher Kevin Winter/Getty Images; Paul Morigi/Getty Images Bill Maher and Byron Allen have a date with Los Angeles City College Foundation. The pair are set for top honors at the institution’s gala — taking place at Four Seasons’ Beverly Wilshire Hotel on Dec. 2 — with Maher poised to receive the Rodney Respect Award while Allen will take home an Impact Award (presented to him by Adam Carolla ). The program, hosted by sportscaster, author and radio journalist Ted Sobel, will also shine a spotlight on Richard and Marjorie Fond, who will receive the Outstanding Alumni Award for their “professional achievements and commitment to education and philanthropy.” Related Stories Lifestyle Harrison Ford Kisses Calista Flockhart on Stage as Couple Receives Their First Joint Award TV After 2026 Midterms, Bill Maher Asks Trump, "Donnie, Are You OK?" The gala has a theme of “Celebrating Resilience,” which the foundation came up with as a way to pay respects to LACC students and how they turn up daily “to overcome obstacles and build better futures.” The foundation will also give them a platform at the event by welcoming LACC student artists to the stage for a musical performance. The Rodney Respect Award is named after late comedy icon Rodney Dangerfield. LACC is home to the Rodney Dangerfield Institute, which offers four classes including a stand-up workshop, improvisational comedy, joke writing and an American film comedy genre class. Maher, long-running host of HBO’s Real Time with Bill Maher , will be feted for his wide-ranging career that includes work as a stand-up comedian, TV host, author, podcaster, political satirist and someone “who has been a defining voice of American comedy and political commentary for more than three decades,” per the foundation. Allen, who was recently honored by Women’s Guild Cedars-Sinai, serves as founder, chairman and CEO of Allen Media Group, which manages a portfolio of such brands as the Weather Channel, HBCUGO, TheGrio Television Network, BuzzFeed and HuffPost, among others. He created and hosts the long-running Comics Unleashed with Byron Allen on CBS. Allen Media Group also produces the gameshow Funny You Should Ask , also airing weeknights on CBS. The Fonds are LACC alumni. Marji, who also graduated from UCLA and Pacifica Graduate Institute, had a career in journalism and publishing with roles at the Los Angeles Times . Rich earned a doctor of pharmacy degree from USC and enjoyed a 41-year career in pharmacy. The Fonds have contributed to LACC and established endowed scholarships at UCLA and USC. LACC is a flagship institution of the Los Angeles Community College District and serves more than 15,000 students. The LACC Foundation provides more than $3 million annually in scholarships, emergency assistance and program support. Gala proceeds support scholarships, stipends, food and emergency assistance and career training resources like tools, equipment and certification fees needed by students pursuing careers in high-demand fields. title: Francis Lawrence Signed On for One ‘Hunger Games’ Movie. Five Films Later, He’s the Keeper of Panem
full_text: × Skip to main content Director Francis Lawrence, Molly McCann as Louella McCoy and Joseph Zada as Haymitch Abernathy in ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.’ Murray Close/Lionsgate Logo text The morning after the New York premiere of The Hunger Games : Sunrise on the Reaping , Francis Lawrence is still taking in the view from the night before. On one red carpet stood nearly every era of Panem. There were the newcomers: Joseph Zada , Whitney Peak and Mckenna Grace, along with franchise first-timers Kieran Culkin, Elle Fanning, Jesse Plemons, Ralph Fiennes and Glenn Close. Tom Blyth, Rachel Zegler and Josh Andrés Rivera who starred in Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes prequel, were in attendance. And there were the originals, Jennifer Lawrence , Josh Hutcherson , Woody Harrelson , Elizabeth Banks, Jena Malone and Willow Shields assembled like the franchise’s own Avengers. Related Stories Movies New 'Hunger Games' Movie on the Way? Lionsgate Film Chief Shares Latest on Franchise's Future Beyond the Book 'Percy Jackson and the Olympians': How Season 3 Brings Epic Moments to Life and Deals With Annabeth's Absence in the Books “Last night at the premiere, for the first time, we had three generations of cast,” Lawrence tells The Hollywood Reporter of the Nov. 16 event. “There’s something really special about the time we’ve all spent together and the quality of people I’ve gotten to work with.” Lawrence has been a constant across all of them. Since taking over from director Gary Ross with 2013’s Catching Fire , he has directed every Hunger Games film that followed, working alongside producer Nina Jacobson to turn Suzanne Collins’ dystopian saga following teenagers forced into fatal combat into one of Hollywood’s most dependable franchises. The original four films grossed roughly $2.98 billion worldwide, and Collins’ five books have sold more than 100 million copies globally, growing into one of the most successful young adult publishing franchises in history. Still, the scale didn’t fully hit him until the final Mockingjay films. Around the release of the films, The Hunger Games: The Exhibition opened to fans, and Lawrence walked through it with his stars. “Walking through it for the first time with Jen and Josh, and I think Liam [Hemsworth] was there, we were all just stunned that we had made something museum-worthy, with our music, our costumes, our props, pieces of our sets and the lore,” he recalls. “There’s something really special in that, knowing these stories have connected with people in a certain way.” Amid the success, it’s easy to forget that Lawrence arrived in Panem as an outsider. He had never made a sequel to someone else’s first film, and on Catching Fire he was “joining an existing family,” with a cast “so big and so seasoned” that he felt he had a lot to prove. He also assumed it would be a one-time job. “The weird thing is, when I signed on to Catching Fire , I thought that was going to be the only one I did,” he says. Instead, the studio asked him to stay for the two-part Mockingjay . “A huge part of me is very appreciative of being invited to keep making these movies and be part of this team.” “There’s something really special about the time we’ve all spent together and the quality of people I’ve gotten to work with,“ Lawrence says of the Hunger Games cast. Mike Coppola/Getty Images That invitation, however, came with a nerve-racking stretch. A few weeks into shooting Mockingjay , production paused for a month so Lawrence and the team could promote and release Catching Fire . He would face its box office verdict with most of the next film’s shoot still ahead of him. “Man, what if this thing bombs?” he remembers thinking of the pressure for Catching Fire success amid filming the third installment. “I now still have like 125 days of shooting with all of these people that are going to be looking at me like, ‘We just made a movie with this guy that bombed.'” He needn’t have worried. After its 2013 release, Catching Fire became the franchise’s highest grossing film, and the once outsider became the keeper of the series. “The series was quite popular at that point, and there was a lot of excitement and confidence at the studio, so that was nice,” he says. When Lawrence and Jacobson returned eight years later with 2023’s The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes , the odds felt less certain. The prequel had no Katniss and centered on the rise of the tyrant Coriolanus Snow, played by Donald Sutherland in the original films with Tom Blyth taking on the role for a younger version. “A bunch of time had gone by, and you wonder if there’s still an appetite for Hunger Games , especially Hunger Games without Katniss,” he says. “It had a very different structure, and it was a story about the person everybody hates, so a lot of things made me a little nervous.” Sunrise on the Reaping , which traces the origins of the fan-favorite mentor Haymitch Abernathy, felt different. “Weirdly, this one I kind of felt less pressure,” Lawrence says. “I felt much more confident that this was one that fans really wanted to see, and it felt like a return to form for movies like Catching Fire and the original.” There being a new Hunger Games book came as a surprise to Lawrence, who assures he, along with Jacobson, are just as in the dark as everyone else. After more than a decade of working together, Lawrence and Collins have a routine. She keeps quiet while she writes, and only once her publisher confirms she has a book does she bring in Lawrence and Jacobson, always with the same modest question of whether the story is a movie. Lawrence and Jacobson always say yes. For Sunrise , Lawrence and Jacobson got word of the novel earlier than ever, and the secrecy was tighter as a result. The manuscript was kept at Collins‘ agent’s home, and then then moved to a locked safe kept with Jacobson. Screenwriter Billy Ray wrote on an offline laptop in Jacobson’s office, while Lawrence stayed busy making secret trips to meet with Collins. “This one we got further in advance, while she was still going back and forth with her editors,” he says. “I had read it a couple of times, Nina had read it a couple of times, and I went to New York to work with Suzanne on breaking down the book into what we thought the movie would be. We hired [original screenwriter] Billy Ray. He was already writing and we were having calls about the draft. So a lot of work was done before the book was even announced, and I couldn’t talk to anybody about it.” The book and its film adaptation were announced together in June 2024, which brought “a lot of relief,” he says. “At least then people knew we were working on it and that it was the Haymitch story. We just had to keep quiet about the storyline itself.” That left the biggest challenge: finding a young Haymitch, the carefree kid from District 12 long before he became the drunken, broken mentor Harrelson made iconic. The search led to Zada, the breakout from Prime Video’s We Were Liars and Netflix’s East of Eden . Lawrence put him “through the wringer” in auditions before landing on the actor to carry the beloved character’s origin story. The seeds for the origin story were “planted over twenty years ago” when Collins began the original trilogy, the author reflected in a letter s hared on social media amid the release of Sunrise . Collins praised Zada’s performance as “remarkably powerful and moving.” From left: Joseph Zada, Plemons, and Lawrence in The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping . Murray Close/Lionsgate *** Long before he was steering a multibillion-dollar franchise, Lawrence spent years making some of the most memorable music videos of the MTV era for artists like Britney Spears, Lady Gaga, Justin Timberlake and Jennifer Lopez. He doesn’t think much about those days when he’s making a movie, he says, but their influence is still there nearly 20 years later. “Having done maybe around 120 videos, it gave me a playground to learn the toolkit I have for making things look a certain way,” Lawrence says. “I got to create different worlds, try different things, learn about visual effects and learn about working with performers. So in terms of visual style, I just had confidence in the image in general: if I imagine something, how can I actually make that happen? Because of videos, that became second nature, so I could focus more on performance and story. That’s probably the biggest way it’s affected my moviemaking in general.” It’s fitting, then, that music runs through Panem. The films have long used it to amplify their themes of resistance. Jennifer Lawrence’s Katniss sings “The Hanging Tree,” which became a rebel anthem. In the prequels, Zegler’s Lucy Gray Baird and Peak’s Lenore Dove are both musicians who capture the hearts of Snow and Haymitch. Lawrence approaches that music the way he approached his videos: “much more music-forward than lyrics-forward.” “I take the mood, tone and feel of a song, and most of the ideas I built for my videos were based on the mood of the song rather than the lyrics. Not always, but I’d say 90 percent of the time. It’s the same here: I’m primarily thinking about the mood, tone and emotional value of music and what I want something to feel like,” he explains. Music is also common ground with Collins. “She’s a real music aficionado with a library in her head, and I had long conversations with her and with [executive music producer and songwriter] Dave Cobb about the creation of songs. She [Collins] usually has a historical background for why and how she wrote certain things, and I would talk to Dave, our music producer, mostly about how I wanted songs to feel. So whether it’s ‘The Hanging Tree,’ a Covey song or ‘The Old Therebefore,’ it’s really about mood,” he says. The music doesn’t stop when the cameras roll. “I also listen to a lot of music when I shoot,” Lawrence says. “Often I’ll be watching a scene with music I have as inspiration playing in my ear, whether it’s score from our movies or from other movies, because I’m evoking a mood, a tone and an emotional value I want to feel in the scene. So sometimes I’m listening to dialogue and to music on my phone at the same time.” His usual choices: The franchise’s scores, of which there are five movies worth, and “Lily’s Theme,” Alexandre Desplat’s piece from Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows – Part 2 . “That has always felt very Hunger Games -ish to me,” he says of the Potter score. “I also listened to some more disturbing stuff for this one, because I thought of it as a bit scarier. Instead of listening to action-oriented music during fight sequences, I’d listen to things that are a little more disturbing and scary. So it was kind of all over the place.“ From left: Liam Hemsworth, Lawrence and Jennifer Lawrence, on set of Catching Fire. Murray Close/©Lionsgate/Courtesy Everett Collection *** Building worlds became Lawrence’s calling card when he made the leap to features. His 2005 debut, Constantine , was a dark take on the DC Comics antihero, and he followed it by envisioning a New York City post-plague for the Will Smith hit I Am Legend (2007). Then came the Great Depression-era romance Water for Elephants (2011), a reunion with Jennifer Lawrence on the spy thriller Red Sparrow (2018), and more recently Slumberland (2022) and the Stephen King adaptation The Long Walk (2025). The genres vary, but in hindsight, the dystopian streak running through several of them looks a lot like a rehearsal for the road to the Panem Capitol. Amid revisiting Hunger Games in the prequels, the director says he’s “trying to” return to where it all began with his first feature, Constantine . It was announced in 2022 that Lawrence would helm a sequel with star Keanu Reeves reprising his role and Akiva Goldsman writing the script. “We have a script,” Lawrence confirms. Part of the appeal of a sequel is getting the band back together. The other part is unfinished business with the ratings board, and this time Lawrence wants to lean into the R rating he once tried to avoid. “We got saddled with an R rating even though we followed all the PG-13 rules, and that was a tough blow,” he says. “On Hunger Games, every time I turn in a cut, it’s an R, we go back and forth a little, and we get to PG-13. With Constantine , they said, ‘We’ve stopped taking notes. There’s no getting a PG-13 on this movie.’ So we were stuck. Part of it was: let’s make another one because we enjoyed it, but this time let’s make the hard-R version. If we’re going to get an R, let’s make the R-rated Constantine .” However, the road to a sequel has been anything but smooth. “We’ve been trying, and we’ve hit roadblock after roadblock,” Lawrence says. “The character was given to somebody to make a network television show, which I never watched, and I don’t think it lasted long.” He continues, “Then J.J. [Abrams] somehow had the rights, or control of the character, for a while and was going to do something with Constantine . But he switched over, and he’s now involved in our project too. He’s a great guy, and he’s pro making this Constantine movie, which is fantastic.”. The other obstacle, Lawrence says, is “there were new people running DC with their own plans for the characters.” Lawrence, Keanu Reeves on Constantine set (2005). Warner Brothers/courtesy Ever Though he doesn’t name anyone, Lawrence notes there has since been a regime change at DC. It was announced on Nov. 9 that James Gunn and Peter Safran are stepping down as co-CEOs of DC studios four years after taking the job. Skydance, which now oversees the division following the acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, has appointed former Marvel exec Jeremy Latcham to the post of president and chief creative officer of DC Studios. With new leadership in place, and with relationships of his own among the executives now running Warner Bros., Lawrence sees an opening. “Maybe there’s some renewed hope to get Constantine through,” he says. “I’m a believer that we could make a sequel to our Constantine with Keanu, and if people at DC wanted to do a different version of Constantine in some sort of shared universe, they could do that, and the two could coexist.” Constantine isn’t the only long-gestating project on his plate. With Sunrise now in theaters, Lawrence is also turning his attention to Red Rising , Pierce Brown’s bestselling sci-fi book series, which he has been developing with the author, a friend, for about eight years. Development of an adaptation first began as a series at Netflix, with two pilot scripts he calls “fantastic,” but it stalled. “There’s just regime changes, and it was an expensive buy-in for them,” he says. “We kept getting shifted around to different departments.” “They never really pulled the trigger,” he adds. “Now there’s a renewed excitement because we’re at Paramount and it’s theatrical again. We have a screenwriter working on it, so I’m very excited.” All roads seemingly lead back to Panem, with Lawrence acknowledging how Red Rising can have a clear thread back to Hunger Games character Plutarch Heavensbee, the Gamemaker turned rebel played by Plemons in Sunrise and the late Philip Seymour Hoffman in the original films. “One of the things that I love about Plutarch is that Plutarch is a bit of an infiltrator,” Lawrence says. Red Rising is an infiltration story too. The story follows Darrow, described as “a rebel forged by tragedy, battling to lead his oppressed people to freedom.” “It allows characters to really question themselves, cross weird moral boundaries and question the people around them. What happens when the people you hate suddenly become more relatable than some of the people that you’re fighting for?” he says. “I’ve always been fascinated by those kinds of stories.” Also on deck is BioShock , an adaptation of 2K Games’ 2007 first-person shooter. “We’re doing a rewrite on a script now,” Lawrence says. “I think that’s getting closer and closer.” In fact, he had a call about the project scheduled for shortly after his conversation with THR . Jesse Plemons and Lawrence in The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping. Murray Close/Lionsgate *** Thirteen years after the Hunger Games franchise began, the odds remain firmly in Panem’s favor. In its opening weekend, Sunrise on the Reaping grossed $120 million , becoming its fourth-best debut in franchise history, besting 2015’s second Mockingjay movie ($102.6 million) and 2023 prequel The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes ($44.6 million) but behind 2013’s Catching Fire ($158 million), 2012’s series-launching The Hunger Games ($152.5 million) and 2014’s first Mockingjay ($121.8 million). For Lawrence, who has lived in this world for more than a decade, the prequels have done more than extend the franchise. They’ve changed how he understands it. “Going through each of these books page by page with Suzanne over time has given me a pretty deep knowledge of the world and the lore. But now that she’s writing these prequels and reframing characters, I’m also learning more each time she releases a book,” he says. He counts himself a fan, but perhaps not the biggest one on set. “I’m sure there are super fans, even people like Mckenna Grace [Maysilee Donner in Sunrise ], who is a super fan of these stories, who know more about all the little nooks and crannies than I do,” he says with a laugh. After so many years of working side by side with Collins, the page and the screen have started to merge in his mind. “The lines between the book and the script start to blur, and you forget what’s just in the movies and what’s exactly from the book,” he says. Plenty of dystopian YA series followed in The Hunger Games ‘ wake, Divergent and The Maze Runner among them, but none has lasted the way Panem has. Lawrence credits Collins’ finger on the pulse of the world as the reason for the story maintaining its popularity. Lawrence and McKenna Grace on set of T he Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping. Murray Close/Lionsgate “Part of what originally separated these books from other YA publications: they had real meat on the bone thematically,” Lawrence says of the story’s lasting appeal. “She also created a world, a narrative and characters people fell in love with: Katniss, Peeta, Effie Trinket. But if they didn’t have the ideas underneath them, they would feel a bit empty and surface-level, and they wouldn’t land the same way. That’s one of the things I feel really lucky about, honestly: we get to make movies that lots of people go to see, but that really have something to say about the world we live in. For me, that’s why they endure.” Does telling this story in today’s climate feel different than it did when the original films came out? “A little bit,” Lawrence says. But the ideas, he argues, have always been built to last. “Suzanne’s original inspiration was watching war footage, then switching channels and seeing reality game shows, and she decided to write this series about the consequences of war for teens. At the time, it was about an idea that was relevant in the moment but also timeless. That’s what she does: she looks at the world and finds ideas that are relevant but weirdly still timeless,” he says. Whether Collins has more to say in Panem is a question only she can answer. In the meantime, the world she built keeps showing up in the real one. Fans dress as the characters at premieres, Lawrence notes, and the films’ songs and three-finger salute have even appeared at protests, “whether it’s Hungary, whether it’s Paris.” “So much of what is created is so disposable,” he says, “and I feel like luckily Hunger Games is not.” From left: Suzanne Collins, Lawrence and Nina Jacobson Dimitrios Kambouris/Getty Images for Lionsgate THR

title: How Netflix and the NFL Hope to Establish New Thanksgiving Eve Tradition With Game and U2 Half-Time Show: ‘We Want to Create Those Global Water Cooler Moments’
full_text: × Continue to Variety SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Nov 24, 2026 11:01am PT How Netflix and the NFL Hope to Establish New Thanksgiving Eve Tradition With Game and U2 Half-Time Show: ‘We Want to Create Those Global Water Cooler Moments’ By Carole Horst Plus Icon Carole Horst Latest Obscured Releasing Picks Up North American Distribution for Finland Oscar Entry ‘The Squirrel’ (EXCLUSIVE) 4 days ago Willa, Women Make Movies Team to Release Shalini Kantayya’s Doc ‘Love Apptually’ Theatrically 6 days ago How Netflix‘s Animated ‘Steps’ Reimagines the Cinderella Story Through the Eyes of Her Asian Stepsisters and Finds a New Kind of Happily Ever After 1 week ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy Netflix Thanksgiving Day has sported NFL games since the league’s inception in 1920, and now Turkey Day tussles on the gridiron are supercharged for the streaming future. On Nov. 25, Netflix and the NFL would like football fans to join them for a new holiday tradition: the Thanksgiving Eve game. And like the streamer’s Christmas Day gridiron matchups, this one is A-list all the way: the Los Angeles Rams vs. the Green Bay Packers at L.A.’s SoFi Stadium and a halftime show headlined by U2. Related Stories ‘PAW Patrol’ Spinoff Series ‘Skye’s Pup Squad’ Set for 2027 Release Gabe Spitzer, Netflix’s VP of global live sports and entertainment, says that cooking up a Thanksgiving Eve game came naturally between Netflix and the NFL. The partners have had great success in the last two years with Christmas Day games, with the matchups hitting 30 million-plus global viewers per game. The focus on showcasing games during holiday periods has conditioned Netflix subscribers and football fans to think of the streamer as a place for out-of-the-ordinary games. “As the NFL opened up more inventory and started talking to us about [possibly adding] more games, [Thanksgiving Eve] is one that they mentioned and immediately it felt like the perfect fit,” says Spitzer, who spoke with Variety while sporting a New England Patriots cap. Onnie Bose, the NFL’s VP of broadcasting, echoes that sentiment. The league has learned “over the last few years that when family and friends are together, they gravitate toward watching our games,” Bose says. “Our Thanksgiving viewership has always been strong. I think it’s exploded. We hit 57 million viewers with the Kansas City-Dallas game last year.” There is precedent for staking out new NFL-watching traditions, as the league has worked closely with Amazon Prime Video over the last few years to successfully establish the Black Friday game on the day after Thanksgiving. “We’ve been building Black Friday with Amazon over the last few years. So Thanksgiving is a clear natural weekend where people are together,” Bose says. “They’re watching football. We’ve seen that on Christmas also in the last few years. We just looked at it as an opportunity to do something new.” It’s been a fruitful marriage between the NFL, which has wants to expand the popularity of football around the world, and the streaming giant with its global footprint in 190 countries. For Thanksgiving Eve, NBC Sports is producing the game broadcast; EverWonder Studio is serving as executive producer for Netflix. Jesse Collins Entertainment, the banner known for handling the Emmy Awards, Oscars and Super Bowl Halftime show, is producing U2’s halftime performance. Netflix’s expanded agreement with the NFL runs through the 2029 season, with a growing presence across the NFL calendar, from Week 1 through Super Bowl week. This year, Netflix streamed the first-ever NFL game played in Australia, a matchup between the San Francisco 49ers and the Los Angeles Rams, on Sept. 10. The NFL also played games in London, Madrid, Munich, Rio de Janeiro, Paris and Mexico City this year. Live sports are a coveted draw for broadcasters and streamers alike. In the U.S., through the Nov. 22 matchup, the NFL has averaged 18.2 million viewers across its broadcasts, its highest mid-season number since 2010. Netflix’s partnership with the league includes Christmas Day games, the NFL’s first regular-season game in Australia, the Thanksgiving Eve game, a Week 18 matchup and the annual NFL Honors awards ceremony. This week’s game marks Netflix’s second time working with the L.A. Rams this season. “Our experience working with Netflix has been fantastic. There is a shared commitment between the Rams and Netflix to put fans first and deliver an exceptional experience, both inside SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, and for audiences watching around the globe,” says Kathryn Kai-ling Frederick, chief marketing officer for the Rams. “Netflix brings a unique ability to combine world-class storytelling, entertainment and live sports, creating opportunities to reach new audiences and elevate the way fans engage with the game. We’re excited to continue building on our relationship and collaborate on moments that extend beyond the field.” The strategy with the NFL is to create lasting moments and cement Netflix in the viewers’ minds as a marquee destination for top games and entertainment. “We’re not the networks that have hundreds of games a year. We’re really showing up intentionally at a few points across the season, and I think this is where Thanksgiving Eve fits in perfectly,” Spitzer says. “We’re that opening game, an international game in Melbourne, Thanksgiving Eve, two games on Christmas and then that final weekend of the season when stakes are all on the line for some of these potential playoff teams.” The Rams and Packers, both with a record of 6-4, are each fighting for a spot in the playoffs, which means that Wednesday’s game has big consequences for both teams’ seasons. Bose says that the Netflix partnership was a natural for the NFL’s plans, especially after seeing how the streamer brought the spotlight to its Christmas Day games. “They’ve truly embraced Christmas. They’ve made it into a big event with their double headers. It’s worldwide distribution. They’ve engaged in putting on concerts,” Bose says. “There’s not a lot of places where we can add new windows where we have partners that are well established in certain places. This was a new window. It fits with their strategy of wanting to have kind of events and standalone windows that resonate.” Spitzer says that Netflix approaches its live events with an eye to setting a high bar in the pop culture landscape. It did that in 2024 with the “Beyoncé Bowl” during the Houston Texans-Baltimore Ravens Christmas Day game, which drew some 27 million viewers in the U.S., not to mention the social media conversation generated by her performance. Beyonce’s revue included Shaboozey, the Texas Southern University’s Oceans of Soul Marching band and a wide range of performers that spoke to Southern Black and Latin history and music. In 2025, Snoop Dogg’s halftime show for Netflix’s Christmas Day games drew 29 million viewers and featured country superstar Lainey Wilson and the hitmakers of “K-pop Demon Hunters”: EJAE, Audrey Nuna and Rei Ami. “Obviously, we’re so early in our live sports journey, but it was a great start,” Spitzer says. With U2, Netflix aims to create another big moment with a band that’s a household name worldwide. “They’ve only done it twice,” Spitzer says about the rock superstars’ NFL game appearances. U2 played in the 2002 game in a moving set that was also a tribute to the victims of 9/11; the other was as an opening act on “Monday Night Football” in 2006 as part of the reopening of the Louisiana Superdome a year after the devastation of Hurricane Katrina. “They want to be a part of a big moment, and we’re thrilled that they want to be on Netflix for launching this new tradition as well,” Spitzer says. The streamer is also bringing celebrity chef David Chang aboard in the pregame show to spotlight food, tailgating and other game-day traditions. For Netflix, it’s as much of a live event strategy as it is a sports strategy. “It’s about creating that new fandom. We want to create those global water cooler moments,” says Spitzer. “That could be a big boxing match. It could be NFL games. It could be the Women’s World Cup, or it could be Alex Honnold climbing a 101-story building. If we’re going to do a big live event, we really want to make sure it cuts through.” Netflix has the rights to the 2027 and 2031 FIFA Women’s World Cup, so lessons learned staging NFL games and other live events look to culminate next year in Brazil. Spitzer won’t comment on whether the streamer is bidding for the 2030 and 2024 Men’s World Cup rights. The Women’s World Cup is “the most ambitious project that we’ve ever done. Thirty straight days, 64 matches over eight hours a day in the U.S. and Canada,” Spitzer says. “We’ve been planning it for two years. There’s nothing bigger, so we can’t wait for that.” For Netflix, aligning with the biggest brand in U.S. sports — the NFL — and creating a new tradition is good for driving global subscriptions and good for the bottom line in a business that has seen layoffs and management shake-ups like every other content giant. For the next few weeks, Team Netflix is all about driving viewership to Thanksgiving Eve and Christmas Day action on the gridiron. “We want to create a new family tradition with Netflix,” Spitzer says. “It’s really about bringing fans together for the biggest moments in sports.” (Pictured: Beyoncé performing at Netflix’s first Christmas Day telecasts of NFL games in 2024) ‘Friends’ Cast Entered Matthew Perry’s Funeral Holding Hands and Cried Around the Casket, Netflix Documentary Reveals David Schwimmer Reunites With His Famous Red Sweater From ‘Friends’ in Nostalgic Quince Campaign Loading comments...
